card.hook: Most bridges are boring in photos. This one bends, so every few steps the railings, cables and valley line up in a new way, and your camera roll fills up fast.
card.stand_here: Stand right where the phone icon is on the map, then face along the curve of the deck so the railing sweeps away from you. Take your first photos here before you wander to either end platform for a look back along the bridge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the curve, the pylon and the cables into one frame. Switch to 1x for people on the bridge, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for faraway hills and sea.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the pylon and cables on one third and the valley on the other, then tap the railing or a person and slide to darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early if you can, because the bridge is likely to be quieter and the summit clearer. Cloud or mist can roll in later and hide the view, so check the weather before you head up.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on one of the triangular platforms at either end, where the bridge stretches out behind you and you can stop without blocking anyone. Try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more of the curve, and hold your phone with both hands. The glass-floor section near the middle is another popular photo spot, and it works for a close selfie looking down into the rainforest.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far end of the bridge beside the triangular platform, while you walk out along the curve so the bridge fills the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay within the designated walkways and don't lean over the edges when you're taking photos. Check the official site before you go for current access, tickets and weather closures.
card.challenge: Take the same view three times, a few steps apart along the curve, and see which one has the best railing line.
card.good_to_know: The bridge hangs from a single tall pylon on top of Gunung Mat Cincang, 660 metres above sea level, and it is 125 metres long. It opened in 2005, closed in 2012 for upgrading, and reopened in 2015. It is for pedestrians only and fairly narrow, so you'll often share the deck.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right where the phone icon is on the map, then face along the curve of the deck so the railing sweeps away from you. Take your first photos here before you wander to either end platform for a look back along the bridge.

card.hook: Picture a rainbow-coloured sign, the Andaman Sea behind it and a crowd of people all waiting for the same sunset. That's Pantai Cenang at the end of the day, and it's a lovely, friendly crush.
card.stand_here: Stand in Pantai Chenang Plaza, the public square at the central beach entrance. Take a few steps back from the rainbow sign so it sits low in your picture, and face west toward the sea.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the sign with the beach and sunset behind it. Try 0.5x if you want more sky and sea, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the sun sitting low over the water.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, then tap the bright sky near the sun and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Around sunset. One blog gives roughly 7.15 to 7.40pm as the usual window, but check the sunset time for your date. Get there early to claim a spot and take your pictures before the sun gets low.
card.selfie_here: Try the rainbow Pantai Chenang sign, directly across from Cenang Mall, where people gather in the evening to watch the sunset. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone allows it on the front) and keep the sign over your shoulder. The big white Langkawi sign at the southern end of the beach is another popular photo stop.
card.rules_and_safety: A listing says selfie sticks are allowed at Pantai Cenang, but it's worth checking on the ground.
card.challenge: Take one sunset shot with the horizon dead level on a gridline, then one where your shadow-dark silhouette beats the sign. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Pantai Cenang is one of Langkawi's best-known stretches of white sand. The plaza is an open public square, and the guides mention no charge. It gets busiest at weekends, so if the crowd is thick, move along the sand and shoot at a slight angle. Casa del Mar is described as a less crowded section with the boardwalk and sea in view.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Pantai Chenang Plaza, the public square at the central beach entrance. Take a few steps back from the rainbow sign so it sits low in your picture, and face west toward the sea.

card.hook: Your boat slows, the engine drops to a mutter, and there it is: the park's name painted in white on a limestone cliff, with turquoise water underneath. It's the picture everyone on the boat grabs, so get your phone out early.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot, at the Kilim Karst Geoforest Park cliff sign. You shoot from the tour boat, facing the sea-facing side of the cliff with the painted name above the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the cliff, the water and a bit of the boat all fit. If the boat stops further away, try zoom 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to bring the lettering closer. Use zoom 0.5x only when you want lots of sea and sky, and keep the cliff away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the painted name on the upper third, and let the water fill the bottom with a corner of the boat in the shot.
card.best_time: Boats usually stop here on the way back, so that's your best chance. Try to shoot when the sun isn't directly in front of the cliff, and ask your tour operator when the stop is likely.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the boat's sea-side deck with the white park lettering on the cliff behind you, use the front camera, and hold your phone steady while the boat pauses. Want a dependable backup? The big park signboard by the Kilim jetty is a popular photo point before you board.
card.ask_someone: Ask a fellow passenger to stay on the front or side of the boat with the cliff sign and turquoise water in frame, while you stand on the deck in front of the lettering.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't encouraged here, and it's not allowed at the Bat Cave. Keep your hands out of the water near the floating fish farms. Check the official site or your tour operator for access, tour details and tide-dependent stops.
card.challenge: Take three quick frames while the boat is slowing, then pick the one where the horizon is level and nobody is blinking.
card.good_to_know: Kilim Karst Geoforest Park is a stretch of limestone cliffs, rivers, mangroves and open sea on Langkawi. Most of it is reached by boat, usually from the Kilim jetty (Jeti Sungai Kilim). Boats may not stop at exactly the same point every trip, so don't count on one perfect angle. If the boat skips the sign, Gorilla Mountain, a limestone outcrop shaped like a gorilla's head and shoulders, makes a good alternative.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot, at the Kilim Karst Geoforest Park cliff sign. You shoot from the tour boat, facing the sea-facing side of the cliff with the painted name above the water.

card.hook: Fish don't pose. You'll line up the perfect shot and the fish will swim off with a flick, so this is a spot for taking lots of frames. Your own reflection in the glass is the other thing to beat.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Underwater World Langkawi itself, so there's no extra walk. Inside, get close to the glass and face the tank square-on, not at an angle.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for big tanks and for a shot of the entrance outside. Zoom 1x suits most single animals, and 2x works for one fish if your phone has it, though it gets softer in dim light.
card.make_it_pop: Press the top of your phone almost against the glass to make most reflections vanish, then tap the animal and slide the brightness down a touch if the bright water looks washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter time of day. Fewer people means easier access to the glass, and one guide recommends off-peak visits for clearer shots without reflections. Outside, daylight gives the best entrance photo.
card.selfie_here: Head into the 15-metre acrylic tunnel tank, where sharks and stingrays pass overhead, and use the front camera at 0.5x so the tank fills the frame above you. Near the entrance, the big Amazonian arapaima tank is a fun spot for a close-up selfie with the largest freshwater fish.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is prohibited throughout because it disturbs the animals. Moray eels and lionfish have sharp teeth and venomous spines, so read the signs before you lean in close to the glass. One older guide lists selfie sticks as allowed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take five quick frames of one fish swimming past, then pick the winner and leave a bit of empty space in front of its nose.
card.good_to_know: Underwater World Langkawi is rank 4 on this map. It's likely a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules. Inside, the walk-through tunnel is a 15-metre acrylic tank.

card.hook: Most people race straight to the sand, but the best frame here is the road that leads to it. Rows of casuarina trees line both sides and point your eye at the sea, like the road is giving you directions.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Tanjung Rhu, the tree-lined road that leads down to the beachfront, and face along it toward the beach. The trees on both sides will lead the eye straight down the middle of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the road and trees. Switch to 0.5x if you want the whole tunnel of trees and the beach at the end, and later try 2x-5x from the beach to pull the limestone islets closer (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the road in the centre so the trees converge, then tap the far end of the road and slide it a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Sunset is the pick for the beach, when the sky colours up behind the limestone islands. Check the tide first if you want wet sand or the sandbar.
card.selfie_here: Walk northeast along the beach from the Tanjung Rhu Resort frontage to the shaded pine trees, then turn back to face the bay. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the bay and beach over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At low tide, stand on the sandbar with the limestone cliffs and clear water behind you, and ask your helper to step back until the whole bay fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The sandbar only appears at certain tides, so plan around that and keep an eye on the water. Take care about jellyfish before swimming, and check locally because parking may be charged and access points may be restricted.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the trees on both sides are perfectly matched, with your friend dead centre on the road like they own it.
card.good_to_know: Tanjung Rhu is a beach on Langkawi where limestone islands rise out of calm, shallow water just offshore. The casuarina (Rhu) trees along the road make natural leading lines, and the road is quieter than the beach. When the sand is wet, it can carry reflections of the sea and sky out towards the islets.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jalan Tanjung Rhu, the tree-lined road that leads down to the beachfront, and face along it toward the beach. The trees on both sides will lead the eye straight down the middle of your shot.

selfie_spots.why: A guide says this stretch is where to take photos, and the pine shade and lush bayshore add an unusual frame to the Tanjung Rhu scenery.

card.hook: Picture a little gondola crawling up a rainforest slope, with the whole green mountain draped around it. That's the shot here, and the cable car line draws a strong diagonal across it for free.
card.stand_here: Stand on the middle station platform, near the SkyBistro cafe, at about 650 m above sea level. Face back down the slope and you'll see the gondolas climbing through the trees, with Oriental Village far below.
card.zoom: Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull one gondola in tight against the trees. Zoom 1x is best for the platform, the slope and the village far below. Zoom 0.5x gets the whole ridge and sky, but the gondolas will look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the gondola line along a diagonal, with the forest filling the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, and probably go earlier, because haze or cloud can cut the view. Check the weather first, as the cars stop in strong winds.
card.selfie_here: Try the Eagle's Nest SkyWalk at the middle station, the cantilevered photo deck. A guide says it gives a more frontal mountain-and-sea angle than the summit decks, and it's quieter. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x with the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Walk to the far end of the Sky Bridge walkway, then ask a passer-by to stand on the bridge and frame the shot so the Sky Cab station shows in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Skip long, extended selfie sticks, because the bridge approach and boarding areas are tight. Stay on the walkways and don't lean over the edges for a photo.
card.challenge: Don't chase a gondola. Frame your shot, then wait for one to glide into the picture along your diagonal, and tap the shutter button the moment it's there.
card.good_to_know: The cable car climbs 2.2 km from Oriental Village at Teluk Burau up Gunung Machinchang, and the ride to the top takes around 15 minutes. It opened to the public in 2002 and was officially opened in 2003. The slope between the base and the middle station is about 42°, said to be one of the steepest of its kind in the world, and the gondolas run roughly 70 metres above the forest canopy.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the middle station platform, near the SkyBistro cafe, at about 650 m above sea level. Face back down the slope and you'll see the gondolas climbing through the trees, with Oriental Village far below.

card.hook: Picture a 91 m ribbon of white water dropping through dark green rainforest, with a cool mist drifting onto your phone screen. That's the lower falls at Telaga Tujuh, and yes, it's as dramatic as it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand at the base of the lower falls, right by the rock pool where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the falls so the whole drop is in front of you, framed by forest on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full height of the falls, the trees and the pool in one go. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the water against the dark rock.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the water, then slide it a little darker so the white water keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. Flowing water looks best, but the weather and season change what you'll see, so your photo may not match other people's.
card.selfie_here: Try the plunge pool at the base of the lower falls, on the rocks at the foot of the 91 m drop, or the red hanging bridge or viewing deck above the falls. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the waterfall behind you, over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back at the lower-pools viewpoint facing the cliff, while you stand in front of the falls so the cascade fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Rocks near the water are slippery, and water can surge down after heavy rain, so move away if the stream rises. Treat the upper infinity pool as a viewpoint only: stay out of the water, as the currents are strong. Entrance fees are unclear, so check with LADA or the tourism board before you go.
card.challenge: Find a leaf or a rock to tuck into the bottom corner of your shot, then see how tiny it makes the waterfall's 91 m drop look.
card.good_to_know: Telaga Tujuh is a waterfall in the Langkawi rainforest. Its lower falls are a single drop of about 91 m into a rock pool, and they're the easiest part to reach. For a wider view of the falls and the forest canopy, try the wooden bridge over the stream, Jambatan Telaga Tujuh.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the base of the lower falls, right by the rock pool where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the falls so the whole drop is in front of you, framed by forest on both sides.

selfie_spots.why: A Langkawi photo guide says the red hanging bridge or viewing deck looks over the whole waterfall and is a good place for pictures.

card.hook: A 12 m eagle is hard to miss, but it's surprisingly hard to squeeze into one phone frame. Eagle Square rewards the person who takes a few steps backwards.
card.stand_here: Head for Eagle Square's walkway and main entrance, right in front of the eagle statue: walk east for about 6-7 minutes on foot. Then pick a spot a good few steps back from the statue and face it, with the star-shaped base in front and Kuah Bay and the boats behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the eagle plus a bit of its surroundings, then tap 0.5x to take in more sky and ground. Save zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the wings and head, so you don't have to stand right underneath.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the eagle, and if the sky starts to wash out, slide the picture a little darker.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually more comfortable and gives softer light. Midday sun can make the statue look harsh.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the walkway in front of the eagle's base, with the statue rising behind you, and use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) to fit more of the bird in. For a different look, try one of the small footbridges in the plaza with the eagle over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand a little to one side of the statue, not directly in front, and ask a passer-by to step back until the whole eagle fits, so the eagle, the sea and the nearby islands all make it in.
card.rules_and_safety: The concrete plaza gets very hot at midday, so early morning or sunset is kinder to your feet. Selfie sticks and flash were reported as allowed, but that info may be out of date, so check on site.
card.challenge: Take one shot from down low at zoom 0.5x and see if you can make the eagle look even taller than it already is.
card.good_to_know: The eagle stands 12 m tall. It sits on a star-shaped base, with Kuah Bay and its boats behind. Take a few frames with and without people, since someone will probably wander through.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Eagle Square's walkway and main entrance, right in front of the eagle statue: walk east for about 6-7 minutes on foot. Then pick a spot a good few steps back from the statue and face it, with the star-shaped base in front and Kuah Bay and the boats behind.

card.hook: Picture a perfect curve of sand, forested hills on one side and a little island parked in the water ahead. That's Datai Bay, and it looks good even in a quick snap.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Datai, the narrow forest road that branches off past The Andaman resort and leads down towards the beach. Face the water, with the foothills on one side and Pulau Anak Datai straight ahead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole curve of the bay and the foothills. Go to 1x for a more natural view, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Pulau Anak Datai.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the island on one of the third-lines, so the curve of the shoreline leads your eye right to it.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the water.
card.selfie_here: Try the headland on Jalan Datai past The Datai resort, where the jungle trail down to the water starts. From this lookout the bay opens up to your right, so use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the beach and water over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The sand is largely reserved for resort guests, so enjoy the view from the public road rather than the beach. Jalan Datai is narrow, so keep to the edge and watch for passing vehicles.
card.challenge: Shuffle a metre or two left or right until the gaps in the trees line up and frame the bay like a picture frame.
card.good_to_know: Datai Bay is a curved bay on Langkawi, with forested foothills on one side and the small island Pulau Anak Datai ahead. Jalan Datai is the public viewpoint and the easiest way to see the whole bay without going into the resort. For a quieter coastal view, Pantai Pasir Tengkorak on the bay's northern side is a free public spot, but check its position on the map before you set out.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jalan Datai, the narrow forest road that branches off past The Andaman resort and leads down towards the beach. Face the water, with the foothills on one side and Pulau Anak Datai straight ahead.

card.hook: One flat white slab on a bright green lawn, with a traditional Malay house behind it. It's a surprisingly calm postcard for such a famous legend.
card.stand_here: Head into the tomb garden at Makam Mahsuri and stand right at the phone icon, in front of the white marble tomb. Face the slab, with the Malay house and trees behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the slab with the house behind it. Go to 0.5x to take in the whole lawn and garden, then 2x for a tighter shot of the house details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the slab level, then tap the white marble and slide it a little darker so the stone keeps its detail instead of going plain white.
card.best_time: There's no fixed time, but morning or later afternoon should give gentler light on the white marble. Fewer visitors then also makes the lawn easier to photograph.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the garden path beside the tomb with the tomb behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the tomb and garden both fit, and hold the phone a bit high.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand on the path in front of the tomb building's exterior, so the whole mausoleum fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine outdoors, but be respectful and don't disturb other visitors. The audiovisual room is off-limits to cameras. Selfie sticks are listed as allowed.
card.challenge: Get the white slab perfectly level on the gridlines with not one stranger in the shot. Patience counts as a skill here.
card.good_to_know: Makam Mahsuri is the tomb of Mahsuri, a young woman at the centre of one of Langkawi's best-known legends. Local tradition says she was executed after being accused of adultery. It's about 12 to 13 km from Kuah (check on the day), and the compound has an entry fee, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into the tomb garden at Makam Mahsuri and stand right at the phone icon, in front of the white marble tomb. Face the slab, with the Malay house and trees behind it.

card.hook: Mount Mat Cincang is way too big to squeeze into a close-up, and that's the fun of it. The trick is to let the beach do the work, with the forested ridge piled up behind it like a giant green curtain.
card.stand_here: Walk onto Pantai Kok, go down to the waterline and turn to face inland. You want turquoise water and sand at your feet and the forested peaks of Gunung Mat Cincang rising behind the beach.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole scene of beach, water and mountain. Then try 2x to pull the peaks closer and make them look taller. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of ripples or footprints up front, and keep the horizon level.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line so the peaks fill the top two thirds, then tap the mountain and slide the brightness down a touch if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go at golden hour. The low light brings out the colour of the water and the texture of the forested slopes. If the sky is hazy the ridge looks flat, so wait a few minutes for a clearer patch.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the mountain behind you, head up by cable car from Oriental Village to the triangular observation platforms at either end of the Langkawi Sky Bridge. Guides call them quieter than the bridge itself, so use the front camera at 0.5x and let the forested mountain and sea sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand on the far-end triangular platform of the Sky Bridge while you pose on the bridge, so they can catch the curve behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: On the Sky Bridge, stay on the designated walkways and don't lean over the edges when taking photos. Selfie sticks are allowed there. The bridge has sometimes been closed for renovation or high wind, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Get a shot where a tiny figure walking along the shore makes the whole mountain look enormous.
card.good_to_know: Mount Mat Cincang is the big forested ridge behind the beaches on the north-west side of Langkawi. The summit hike is strenuous, but this photo doesn't need it because everything here is taken from beach level. Pantai Kok is an open public beach, said to be open 24 hours with free entrance (check locally), while the cable car and summit are paid and separate. For a different view, Pantai Burau shows the bay with the mountains across the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk onto Pantai Kok, go down to the waterline and turn to face inland. You want turquoise water and sand at your feet and the forested peaks of Gunung Mat Cincang rising behind the beach.

card.hook: Picture a beach that curves like a lazy smile, with palms or casuarina trees leaning in and the Andaman Sea filling the background. That's Pantai Tengah, and it's made for holiday photos.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right on Pantai Tengah beach. For a higher view, walk to the northern end where the coastal rocks are, then face down the coastline so the beach curves away below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sweeping curve of the beach. Go to 0.5x for more sea and sky, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the offshore islands or boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the curve of the shoreline along one third of the frame, and keep the horizon level so the sea and sky fill the rest.
card.best_time: Go at dusk. The shoreline faces west, so the sun sets right over the sea, and the trees on the sand make a natural frame. If the sky looks too bright, tap the sea and slide it a little darker to keep the colour.
card.selfie_here: Try the quieter stretch of sand at sunset, with the sea behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the sunset over your shoulder. A pink bean bag was set out there in one photo, but it's a prop, so bring your own or ask a café. Another good backdrop is the 'Hidden' sign on the white wall at the beachside dining area of Hidden Langkawi.
card.rules_and_safety: Only one guide mentions the rocks at the northern end, so check they're still easy to climb when you arrive, and take care on them.
card.challenge: Get the whole curve of the beach in one shot with a perfectly level horizon. Then see if you can do it again with a palm tree framing one side.
card.good_to_know: Pantai Tengah is on the west coast of Langkawi's main island, along Jalan Pantai Tengah. One guide says it's about 700 m long. Near the island-hopping pier you can also photograph colourful boats with green hillsides behind them, but check the exact pier on the map.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right on Pantai Tengah beach. For a higher view, walk to the northern end where the coastal rocks are, then face down the coastline so the beach curves away below you.

selfie_spots.why: The beach faces west and is less crowded than Pantai Cenang, so a visitor can shoot at sunset with the sand and sea in the frame.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence. No page I found names a precise point on the beach where the whole beach is in frame for a passer-by photo, so ask_someone_spot is null. The Pantai Tengah island-hopping pier is named (mel365), but no page says it gives a full view of the beach. The 'Panorama viewpoint' mentioned on mel365 is not tied to a location, so I left it out. The Lemon8 pages are in Malay, and the Hidden Langkawi sign detail comes from a Malay caption. No page gave selfie-stick or tripod rules, and the tripod mention on Bambu Langkawi is a shooting tip, not a rule. The coordinates you gave (6.28459, 99.73201) roughly match the Tengah Beach GPS on Travelfish (about 6.280 N, 99.730 E), so the area is right. Pages do not say which way the visitor should face, so orientation is left to the user.
